Thank you for your feedback and insightful suggestions on our work. We are committed to continuously improving CleanDiffuser in line with your advice. Here are our responses to the questions you've raised:

- **Q1:Why not build CleanDiffuser (CD) upon Huggingface Diffusers (HD)?** 

One of our initial motivations for developing CD was the extreme difficulty in implementing decision-making algorithms using HD. In fact, very few works in the decision-making community use HD for their code. The main differences are: (1) **Huggingface Diffusers organizes its library by paper.** We can easily use many famous diffusion models (e.g. DDIM, ControlNet, DiT, Stable Diffusion) provided by HD to generate awesome images. However, these works can not be straightly used to develop decision-making algorithms. **CleanDiffuser is organized by functionality**. This allows us to easily transfer features in DDIM (as a solver), ControlNet (as a fine-tuning method), DiT (as a neural network backbone), and Stable Diffusion (as a VAE-Diffusion architecture) to develop decision-making algorithms. The organizational logic of HD and CD is completely different, and they target different user groups. We believe that Huggingface Diffusers is aimed at users who want to quickly use diffusion models to generate high-quality multimedia data. In contrast, CleanDiffuser is for users who want to quickly combine diffusion building blocks to develop their own decision-making algorithms. (2) **CleanDiffuser provides numerous decision-specific features that directly affect the coding logic of diffusion models**. Thus, the diffusion part in CD is entirely designed around decision-making, structurally different from image generation diffusion models. **The organizational logic of the libraries and their intended users significantly differ between Huggingface Diffusers and CleanDiffuser, making their integration currently impractical.**


- **Q2:Moving Related Works to the Main Text.**

 We apologize for any confusion caused by placing the related works in the Appendix, potentially making the main text challenging to understand. We will adjust the content in the revision, moving related works to the main text. Thank you for the suggestion!


- **Q3: Adding Unit Testing.**

 We are currently undergoing a major update to a PyTorch Lightning version (as mentioned in the universal rebuttal), within the **lightning** branch of our GitHub repository. This major update will introduce unit testing. Your suggestion is invaluable, indeed facilitating future code updates significantly!


- **Q4:About Documentation and Suggestions for Jupyter Note Tutorials.**

 We deeply regret the lack of documentation. Following the submission of CleanDiffuser, we excessively focused on adding new content (as mentioned in the universal rebuttal above) and neglected the supplementation of documentation, which was a mistake. We are actively amending this error. You can now find two updated Jupyter Notebook format tutorials on our GitHub repository, which can be executed cell by cell and come with detailed explanations **(we look forward to you reading these notebooks and providing feedback, which will guide our subsequent updates! : ) ).** We are also updating more documentation. The updates to tutorials and documentation will continue throughout the rebuttal phase (due to the substantial workload, it cannot be completed in a few days). **We will pause ongoing code development to prioritize improving documentation. Thank you for your patience and understanding.**


- **Q5:Why the pipelines are put outside of the main library?** 

From a model perspective, in the decision-making domain, diffusion models play a role vastly different from other domains (e.g., image generation). They might be used to generate actions, trajectories, action chunks, motion sequences, transitions, and need to consider the future impact in terms of time dimension. This is unlike image generation, which solely requires producing static images. Hence, in decision-making, the application of diffusion models is more flexible, with each algorithm in the pipelines providing a novel and effective method of use. We hope they serve as examples to inspire users to develop new methods. From a coding perspective, the main library offers a wealth of building blocks, with the algorithms in the pipelines combining these building blocks. We hope this serves as an example to help users learn how to combine building blocks. For these reasons, we decided to keep the pipelines as a separate part from the main library. We believe this also shows our different library organizational logic from the Huggingface Diffusers.


- **Q6:How to validate the algorithms' implementations?**

We compare our implementations with official implementations on the same benchmarks, ensuring at least a comparable performance. Additionally, we record key variables during training and inference to ensure their numerical validity. From current results, our implementations achieve or even surpass the official versions while being cleaner. So we believe the implementations are well-validated.

One of our initial motivations for developing CD was the extreme difficulty in implementing decision algorithms using HD. In fact, very few works in decision-making community use HD for their code. The main differences are: (1) **Huggingface Diffusers organizes its library by paper.** We can easily use many famous diffusion models (e.g. DDIM, ControlNet, DiT, Stable Diffusion) provided by HD to generate awesome images. However, these works can not be straightly used to develop decision-making algorithms. **CleanDiffuser is organized by functionality**. This allows us to easily transfer features in DDIM (as a solver), ControlNet (as a fine-tuning method), DiT (as a NN backbone), and Stable Diffusion (as a VAE-Diffusion architecture) to develop decision-making algorithms. The organizational logic of HD and CD is completely different, and they target different user groups. We believe that HD is aimed at users who want to quickly use diffusion models to generate high-quality multimedia data. In contrast, CD is for users who want to quickly combine diffusion building blocks to develop their own decision-making algorithms. (2) **CleanDiffuser provides numerous decision-specific features that directly affect the coding logic of diffusion models**. The diffusion part in CD is entirely designed around decision-making, structurally different from image generation diffusion models.

**Q2:About the name "Diffuser"**

 It was inspired by the 'Diffuser' method, with the "er" suffix making it sound like an agent using diffusion for decision-making. This naming influenced subsequent decision agents like "MetaDiffuser", "AdaptDiffuser", etc. CleanDiffuser for us means a "Clean" library for developing "Diffusers". We acknowledge the names are just tangled together, and we will consider changing the name in future updates.

**Q3:About scores in Table 1**  

We apologize for the confusion. As CleanDiffuser focuses on diffusion decision-making models, the score reports for BC and LSTM-GMM are cited from previous papers. Although we didn't reproduce these two algorithms ourselves, the benchmark and validation methods are the same. We're confident that the experimental comparisons are fair. Following your suggestion, we'll emphasize the sources of all numbers and add score comparisons between our implementations and official ones in the revision.

**Q4:Comparison of guidance techniques**   
We appreciate your suggestion. It is a meaningful ablation experiment. Different from image generation, guidance techniques in decision-making have **highly flexible uses**, such as using Q-value/Return to improve optimality, using observation to generate actions at the moment, and using dynamics to enhance the legality of generated trajectories, etc. Thus, it is challenging to compare the merits of classifier guidance (CG) and classifier-free guidance (CFG) across all uses. We chose Return as the guidance for an example, as it is one of the most commonly used ones. We implement two diffusion planners with different guidance but identical other aspects (neural network backbone, diffusion backbone, sampling steps, etc.), with the results in the table below. (**Note:** The additional classifier trained for CG is a return predictor that can serve as a critic for planning, i.e., generating k trajectories in parallel and selecting the one with the highest return, so **CG-k** in table indicates how many trajectories are generated for planning. Since CFG lacks the classifier, it is equivalent to k=1). We find that CFG performs better than CG at k=1, and as k increases, CG's performance generally goes through a rise and fall. We suspect that the classifier leads to a reward hack, where the selected highest-return trajectory might lack legality and cannot be correctly executed. Moreover, using CG requires computing the network's gradient at each sampling step, which is three times slower than CFG in our experiments, and even slower for larger k, which is detrimental for tasks with specific decision frequency requirements. Therefore, we believe CFG has certain advantages over CG in return guidance. However, this does not mean CG is useless; in fact, many works have improved CG, such as optimizing with contrastive learning, allowing CG to perform comparably to CFG in specific uses. Thank you again for the insightful suggestion, we’ll further supplement these types of experiments in our revision.

Thank you for your positive feedback and your insightful suggestions. We'll continue to improve CleanDiffuser based on your advice. Here are our responses to your questions:

**Q1: Why noise prediction?** 

Thank you for pointing that out! It seems the name "noise prediction" may have caused some misunderstanding, we will provide detailed explanations in the revised version. Noise prediction refers to **using a neural network (NN) to predict the noise $\epsilon_\theta$ added to the data at each denoising step**. It's not actually "noise" in the true sense. Mathematically speaking, whether it's noise prediction or data prediction, both are using NNs to approximate an affine-transformed score function - they're essentially the same. 

However, in practice, different prediction methods can affect algorithm performance. This impact lacks systematic research. For example, the Diffuser[1] algorithm uses data prediction by default, while the DD[2] algorithm uses noise prediction. So we implement the two prediction ways as a switch to highlight a potential research direction. 

**Q2: BC with diffusion NN backbone.**

We completely agree that BC and diffusion policies can perform similarly on simple tasks if diffusion policies are only trained to imitate. However, in RL, diffusion policies incorporate many RL techniques that allow them to gradually learn the optimal policy from the behavior policy, ultimately making them significantly better than BC (behavior policy).       

Also, we believe it's meaningful to include a BC using a diffusion NN backbone as a baseline to assess how much performance gain comes from the NN backbone. Therefore, we implement a **BC with IDQL's NN backbone (LNResnet**, a residual MLP structure with layer normalization) and compared it with the **BC in Table 1 (using a 3-layer MLP)**. # Universal Rebuttal

Dear Reviewers,

We're very grateful for each reviewer's thoughtful feedback and insightful suggestions. Your valuable feedback will greatly help us improve the CleanDiffuser library. We've carefully read through all the reviews and addressed every question raised in this rebuttal. We sincerely hope this resolves any concerns. If you have any further questions after reading our response, please don't hesitate to comment - we'll get back to you as soon as possible.

Since our paper submission, CleanDiffuser has been continuously evolving. **Our GitHub repo has now garnered 262 stars and 21 forks, receiving lots of positive feedback and collaboration requests from researchers in the decision-making community**. Compared to the submission version, we've added the following new features:

- **Consistency Models:** We've implemented both consistency training and consistency distillation. Our consistency training implementation refers to the improved version, which delivers better performance.
- **Consistency IDQL policy:** We’ve implemented a consistency-model-based IDQL for demonstration. To our knowledge, CleanDiffuser is the **first** library allowing developers to modularly use consistency training or distillation in decision algorithms.
- **ACT:** We’ve implemented an ACT (Action Chunking Transformer) with CleanDiffuser. This addition enables easy comparison between transformer-based and diffusion-based BC.
- **Two new pipeline algorithms:** We’ve added **DiffuserLite** and **SfBC** into `pipelines`. We're continuously adding state-of-the-art algorithms, with **QGPO** nearly complete and coming soon.
- **New tutorials:** Following suggestions from reviewers QWaA and WBYx, we're revamping tutorials using **Jupyter Notebooks**, which will be hosted on Colab for a more user-friendly experience.
- **Code refactoring using PyTorch Lightning:** As more and more decision-making researchers delve into embodied AI research, using larger, more complex datasets, advanced deep learning techniques like **multi-GPU parallelism and mixed precision** are becoming crucial. PyTorch Lightning offers super simple APIs for these features while maintaining compatibility with PyTorch. We believe this will greatly benefit CleanDiffuser users. This major update is about 60% complete - you can check our progress on the **'lightning' branch** of our GitHub repo. During this update, we're also addressing reviewer suggestions by **adding unit tests, more algorithms**, and other improvements.

We hope this progress list shows our commitment to making CleanDiffuser awesome. Many reviewers point out issues with our documentation, and we sincerely apologize for this oversight. We've been so focused on adding new features that we neglected proper documentation, which was a mistake. We've partially improved the docs and are continuously updating them. We promise to pause feature development and prioritize completing the documentation and tutorials to lower the barrier to entry. Rest assured, CleanDiffuser will continue to be updated, and we'll keep doing our best to contribute to the diffusion decision-making community.

Once again, thank you for your thorough reviews and insightful suggestions. We appreciate your patience and look forward to addressing any remaining concerns.

Sincerely,

Authors

summary_and_contributions.value: The paper introduces an open-source library that facilitates the implementation of diffusion models for decision-making tasks. The library benchmarks multiple algorithms, including planners that generate long-term trajectories, policies that output actions based on states, and data synthesizers for data generation. The implemented models include DDPM, DDIM, EDM, Rectified flow models, DPM-solver, and DPM-solver++. Additionally, the library incorporates an adaptive masking strategy and various tricks to improve the efficiency of diffusion models.

review.value:
The paper provides a valuable resource by benchmarking different algorithms within a unified framework, which can aid researchers in this field.

However, there are some points needing clarification:
- The reason behind implementing noise/data prediction as a switch is unclear. What scenarios require the model to generate noise?
- There are existing papers finding that BC and diffusion policy might perform similarly when the task is simple. Hence I think the comparison between diffusion models and BC should be based on the same architecture. Additionally, sampling steps of 2 or 3 are enough for simple tasks like picking and placing to generate good actions. Rectified flow might be better than DDPM or DDIM in this case since the learned ODE is straight. 
Overall, this paper is a good read and will positively impact the field of diffusion-based decision-making due to its current popularity.

strengths.value: This work is well-written and presents a good benchmark for different diffusion/flow-based policy learning methods.

summary_and_contributions.value: This paper provides CleanDiffuser, a new library for unifying diffusion-based decision-making methods. The authors provide the implementation of various algorithms, neural networks and interface with the simulation environments. There are reproduced benchmarking results and new analyses with the proposed CleanDiffusers library. The library is open-sourced, but the documentation is unfinished.

review.value:
1. Quality: I admit that currently diffusion-based decision The paper provides a nice overview of previous methods and fair benchmarking. There is an accompanying library which is coded neatly.
2. Clarity: The writing is clear and easy to understand.
3. Originality: Libraries for diffusion models are everywhere. The main originality of the proposed library is that it is specific to decision-making tasks. In my opinion: (1) the diffusion part overlaps with huggingface Diffusers; (2) the network structure part are new because they are the new structures proposed in decision-making papers; (3) Environment interface overlaps with existing imitation learning/offline RL libraries.

Although one can conduct all the experiments in this paper by assembling existing libraries, I admire the efforts of this paper to attempt to unify decision-making diffusion models. The current status of the area is chaotic with many diverse claims. I think the contribution of the paper is solid, but I still concern whether people will do fair comparison with this new library.
4. Significance: This paper is a good step-forward for fair quantitative empirical evaluation of the field.

strengths.value:
1. The proposed library aligns different papers in the diffusion-based decision-making field. It also includes new diffusion algorithms such as rectified flow.
2. The benchmarking is thorough. The experiments in Table 2 and Figure 6 are interesting, giving new possible research directions.
3. Writing is very good. The library is coded in a neat style.

opportunities_for_improvement.value:
1. Name: CleanDiffuser is not related to decision-making. It makes me very confused because the huggingface Diffusers library is the de facto standard library for diffusion models. CleanDiffuser sounds like a lite version of the Diffusers library. Besides, there are methods called 'Diffuser', "AdaptDiffusers". All these names are just tangled together.

2. Table 1: To make sure the numbers are reliable, I compared Table 1 with the original Table 2 in "Planning with Diffusion for Flexible Behavior Synthesis". I found: (1) BC numbers are directly copied; (2) The reproduced result of Diffuser-Medium-Replay-Walker2d (58.3) is worse than the original paper (70.6). I suggest the authors to (1) clearly note which numbers are adopted from other papers, because they are actually not comparable to the numbers reproduced with the proposed library; (2) provide the original numbers to help readers compare the implementation in this paper with the original results.

3. Analyses: For a new paper, readers expect to see new results. I like Section 5.3 and 5.4 as they discuss the impacts of implementation details. From my personal viewpoint, since the proposed library provided classifier guidance and classifier-free guidance, it would be interesting to perform ablation study on this guidance techniques in decision-making scenarios. It is widely known that they are important in text-to-image generation, but as far as I know, impacts of them in decision making is unknown.

summary_and_contributions.value: In this paper, the authors introduce *CleanDiffusers*, an open-source python library designed for decision making algorithms with Diffusion Models. They also demonstrate the usability of their library through a benchmark where several algorithms are considered.

review.value: To me this is a significant contribution but I still wonder if the entry barrier to use the library is not too high. I think a polished documentation and more didactic tutorials would definitively help the library adoption. Moreover, I still advise the authors to try to address the points raised in section **Opportunities For Improvement** that will, in my opinion, make the paper even stronger but more importantly will also ensure a better robustness to changes of the library though time.

strengths.value:
To me, this contribution and more generally, contributions involving open-source libraries aiming at unifying existing approaches and comparing them in a controlled environment are significant contributions. They are crucial to allow research moving forward since they allow fair methods benchmarking but also allow methods to remain maintained and available though time.

The library provides a modular testing environment that allows a support of many different algorithms and allows apparently switching easily several blocks such as the diffusion backbones for instance, which reveal useful for benchmark and comparison purposes  

I am not an expert of decision-making algorithms but to me the benchmark performed seems sound.

opportunities_for_improvement.value:
### Paper

- Why the authors decide not to build their framework upon the existing and quite comprehensive *diffusers* library? From what the authors explain, it seems that this library could be integrated in their framework that would benefit from existing blocks already implemented.

- I know that page number limit is tight but I think that the related works section included in section B should instead be part of the paper. 

### Library
- I strongly advise the authors to also include unit testing to their framework. This would ensure seamless integration of any new piece of code.

- The online documentation should be polished since many elements are still missing.

- Why did the author chose the put the pipeline outside of the main library? Are these intended to only be examples?

- How did the authors validate their diffusion-based decision-making algorithms implementations? 

- I wonder if adding notebook tutorials instead (or in addition) to the documentation would help the adoption of the library?

limitations.value: The main limitation that I see is the potential entry barrier to allow a wide adoption of the library since while being modular, creating a pipeline involves quite a good knowledge of the library. Moreover, the lack of unit tests can make the code quite unreliable through time if new features are continuously added.

title.value: CleanDiffuser: An Easy-to-use Modularized Library for Diffusion Models in Decision Making

TLDR.value: We present CleanDiffuser, the first diffusion model library specifically design for decision making.

abstract.value: Leveraging the powerful generative capability of diffusion models (DMs) to build decision-making agents has achieved extensive success. However, there is still a demand for an easy-to-use and modularized open-source library that offers customized and efficient development for DM-based decision-making algorithms. In this work, we introduce **CleanDiffuser**, the first DM library specifically designed for decision-making algorithms. By revisiting the roles of DMs in the decision-making domain, we identify a set of essential sub-modules that constitute the core of CleanDiffuser, allowing for the implementation of various DM algorithms with simple and flexible building blocks. To demonstrate the reliability and flexibility of CleanDiffuser, we conduct comprehensive evaluations of various DM algorithms implemented with CleanDiffuser across an extensive range of tasks. The analytical experiments provide a wealth of valuable design choices and insights, reveal opportunities and challenges, and lay a solid groundwork for future research. CleanDiffuser will provide long-term support to the decision-making community, enhancing reproducibility and fostering the development of more robust solutions.

def process(client, invitation):

    domain = client.get_group(invitation.domain)
    venue_id = domain.id
    submission_venue_id = domain.content['submission_venue_id']['value']
    venue_name = domain.content['title']['value']

    now = openreview.tools.datetime_millis(datetime.datetime.utcnow())
    cdate = invitation.cdate

    if cdate > now:
        ## invitation is in the future, do not process
        print('invitation is not yet active', cdate)
        return

    def post_submission_edit(submission):

        updated_note = openreview.api.Note(
            id=submission.id
        )

        if invitation.edit['note']['readers'] == ['everyone'] and submission.odate is None:
            updated_note.odate = now
            updated_note.content = {
                '_bibtex': {
                    'value': openreview.tools.generate_bibtex(
                        note=submission,
                        venue_fullname=venue_name,
                        year=str(datetime.datetime.utcnow().year),
                        url_forum=submission.forum,
                        paper_status='under review',
                        anonymous='readers' in submission.content['authors'] or 'readers' in invitation.edit.get('note', {}).get('content', {}).get('authors', {})
                    )
                }
            }

        client.post_note_edit(
            invitation=invitation.id,
            note=updated_note,
            signatures=[venue_id]
        )
    
    ## Release the submissions to specified readers if venueid is still submission
    submissions = client.get_all_notes(content= { 'venueid': submission_venue_id })
    print(f'update {len(submissions)} submissions')
    openreview.tools.concurrent_requests(post_submission_edit, submissions, desc='post_submission_edit')
